pronunciation.note: Hoori is Tier 2 in this restoration: the long ō is not represented, so the ASCII form is identical to Hepburn. He is a pivotal ancestor in the imperial genealogy.

domains.title: Fire-Subduing Prince and Imperial Ancestor
domains.subtitle: Hunter, Sea-Voyager, and Founder of the Royal Line
domains.lead: Hoori is the younger son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime, the husband of the sea princess Toyotama, and the great-grandfather of Japan's first emperor, Jimmu. His name, 'Fire-Subduing,' marks him as the brother who overcame Hoderi's fire and whose line would rule the land.

cards.name: Master of the Mountains
cards.desc: He received the bow and became a hunter of the highlands.

cards.name: Husband of Toyotama
cards.desc: Married the daughter of the sea god Ryūjin in the undersea palace.

cards.name: Father of Ugayafukiaezu
cards.desc: His son by Toyotama continued the line to Emperor Jimmu.

cards.name: Imperial Forebear
cards.desc: His story explains how the imperial line gained legitimacy from both sea and land.

mythology.lead: Hoori's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly descent of Ninigi and the earthly reign of Jimmu. It is a story of exile, marriage, and return.

myths.title: The Lost Fishhook
myths.text: After exchanging gifts with his brother Hoderi, Hoori received the fishhook but lost it in the sea. Hoderi refused any substitute. Desperate, Hoori descended to the undersea palace of Ryūjin, the dragon god of the sea, where he was welcomed and married to the sea god's daughter, Toyotama.

myths.title: The Promise and the Broken Taboo
myths.text: Toyotama agreed to accompany Hoori to land on the condition that he not watch her give birth. Curiosity overcame him; he peeked and saw her in her true form as a sea dragon or crocodile. Ashamed, Toyotama returned to the sea, leaving their son Ugayafukiaezu to be raised on land. She sent her sister Tamayori to care for the child.

myths.title: Founder of the Line
myths.text: Ugayafukiaezu married his aunt Tamayori, and their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, later known as Emperor Jimmu. Thus Hoori's voyage to the sea and back became the mythical foundation of the imperial line.

lore.syncretism: Hoori's story fuses several themes common across East Asia: the mortal who visits the dragon palace, the animal bride whose true form must not be seen, and the younger brother who supersedes the elder. These motifs have parallels in Chinese, Korean, and Ainu narratives, but in Japan they were organized into a single genealogy culminating in the emperor.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hoori is remembered chiefly as an ancestor, but his story has inspired countless retellings. The dragon-palace motif appears in folk tales, Noh plays, and modern fiction. His descendants' claim to rule both land and sea shaped Japanese political mythology for centuries.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hoori is the one who looked. His curiosity cost him the presence of his divine wife, yet it also produced the imperial line. His story suggests that legitimacy is born not from perfect obedience but from the risks taken in pursuit of knowledge and connection.
lore.archaeology: Hoori has no independent material cult. His significance is textual, preserved in the Kojiki's narrative of imperial origins and in the genealogical claims of the Yamato state.
